title: Cross-Boundary Wildfire Solutions Act
summary: This bill orders the Government Accountability Office to study how federal programs and rules help or get in the way of fighting wildfires across property lines — where federal land, state land, private land, and tribal land all meet. The GAO must report its findings and recommendations to Congress within two years. The bill itself makes no change to wildfire programs; it only commissions the study.
brief: Directs the Comptroller General (GAO) to study and report within two years on federal programs and rules that enable or inhibit wildfire mitigation across land-ownership boundaries.

top_lines.headline: GAO Wildfire Study
subs: GAO studies federal programs and rules affecting cross-boundary wildfire mitigation
Examines whether changes would give agencies, states, local, and Tribal governments more funding or capacity
Reviews activities carried out under a covered authority to improve wildfire mitigation and forest health

top_lines.headline: Report to Congress
subs: GAO report due within 2 years of enactment
Must include recommendations to simplify cross-boundary wildfire mitigation

likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Neguse (D-CO) with a bipartisan group of cosponsors (Kim, Harder, Obernolte), the bill orders only a GAO study with no spending or regulatory mandate, which lowers opposition. Its bipartisan backing and low cost leave it little to fight over, though as a study-only bill its Senate scheduling is uncertain.

items.main: Names the Act the “Cross-Boundary Wildfire Solutions Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Defines the terms 'covered agency' and 'covered authority' used in the study.
items.detail: 'Covered agency' means each federal land management agency, the Natural Resources Conservation Service, the Environmental Protection Agency, FEMA, the U.S. Fire Administration, states, Indian Tribes, and local governments. 'Covered authority' means the Healthy Forests Restoration Act of 2003, the Cooperative Forestry Assistance Act of 1978, the good neighbor authority under the Agricultural Act of 2014, the Tribal Forest Protection Act of 2004, the collaborative forest landscape restoration program under the Omnibus Public Land Management Act of 2009, and any other statutory authority that facilitates cross-boundary wildfire mitigation or forest-health improvement, as determined by the Comptroller General.

sections.label: Section 3 — Study on Wildfire Mitigation Across Land Ownership Boundaries

items.main: Requires the Comptroller General to study existing federal programs, rules, and authorities that enable or inhibit wildfire mitigation across land-ownership boundaries on federal and non-federal land.
items.detail: The study must examine whether changes to any program, rule, or authority — including changes to existing statutory definitions — would give a covered agency (federal land management agencies, the Natural Resources Conservation Service, the Environmental Protection Agency, FEMA, the U.S. Fire Administration, states, Indian Tribes, and local governments) increased capacity or access to funding to mitigate wildfires or improve forest health, and would enable better community protection and prevent the loss of structures due to wildfire. It must also review the activities carried out under a covered authority, including how to improve their efficacy at mitigating wildfire and whether enacting that authority increased a covered agency's capacity or access to wildfire-mitigation funding.

items.main: Requires a report to Congress within two years of enactment containing the study results and recommendations.
items.detail: The report goes to the House Committees on Natural Resources and on Agriculture and the Senate Committees on Energy and Natural Resources and on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. It must include recommendations to simplify cross-boundary wildfire mitigation between federal land management agencies and state, local, and Tribal governments.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Neguse
featured_quotes.text: first, I thank my colleague from New Mexico for her steadfast leadership, for the work that she has done as a champion for the Southwest, the great State of New Mexico, and, of course, her leadership on all matters connected to science. I am grateful to her for her steadfast leadership and commitment. I certainly echo his remarks, the remarks from Representative Stansbury, and, of course, the remarks of Ranking Member Huffman, as well. It has been said, but I think it bears repeating: Wildfires do not care if lands are Federal, State, or local.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Westerman
featured_quotes.text: to address the enormity of the wildfire crisis, it is critical that we find ways to improve forest management across manmade jurisdictional boundaries. H.R. 3922 is a good bipartisan bill that will do just that by identifying existing Federal policies that can be changed to streamline proactive forest management.

gaps: The bill commissions a study and recommendations on cross-boundary wildfire mitigation but does not direct any agency to act on the recommendations.
The bill requires the report within two years but specifies no funding for conducting the study.
The bill examines access to wildfire-mitigation funding but does not itself authorize or appropriate any mitigation funds.

added: A Comptroller General study on cross-boundary wildfire mitigation programs, rules, and authorities, with a report to Congress due within two years of enactment
New definitions section defines 'covered agency' (federal land agencies, NRCS, EPA, FEMA, U.S. Fire Administration, States, Indian Tribes, local governments)

New 'covered authority' definition lists the Healthy Forests Restoration Act, Cooperative Forestry Assistance Act, good neighbor authority, Tribal Forest Protection Act, collaborative forest landscape restoration program, plus any other facilitating authority
EPA added to the list of agencies whose capacity/funding access the study examines
Study must now also assess whether changes would 'enable better community protection and prevent the loss of structures due to wildfire'
Report must now also go to the House Agriculture Committee and the Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
modified: Study scope generalized from the specific section 103(e) Healthy Forests activities to activities under any 'covered authority', and now covers wildfire mitigation or forest-health improvement
Change analysis now explicitly includes 'changes to existing statutory definitions'
